meta.title: Pipe Fitting Moulds & Tooling — Plumbing | Metal Form
meta.description: Tooling and engineering for plastic pipe fittings: elbows, tees, sockets, threaded adapters, valve bodies and drainage parts. Collapsible and unscrewing cores, high-cavitation and modular family tooling, second-source moulds. Since 2006.

name: Plumbing & Construction
tile: Fitting families where one tooling logic has to serve forty part numbers. Threads, sealing geometry, unscrewing and collapsible cores, and dimensional consistency across the range.

headline: A fitting range is a tooling problem
before it is a catalogue.
hero.lead: Elbows, tees, sockets, threaded adapters, valve bodies, push-fit, electrofusion and drainage parts. Send the dimension table, the material and the annual volume. We return the tooling route, the cavitation, the mechanism and the part weight.
markers: Modular frames for the SKU tail

plate.label: Range plate · one grid, one scale
plate.note: Twelve fitting types drawn to one another's scale in hairline outline. Teal is polymer. Brass is metal. Every drawing on this page holds to that.

range.heading: One geometry, nine diameters, twelve configurations.
range.body: A working fitting range is typically 200 to 900 live part numbers. A handful of them carry most of the volume. The rest carry most of the tooling cost. That imbalance is the sector's defining commercial problem, and it is a tooling problem long before it is a catalogue problem.
range.body2: Below is a range shape drawn as a matrix: twelve fitting types across nine nominal diameters. It is an illustration of how a range proliferates, not a Metal Form project and not a proposal for yours.

views.name: One tool per part number
views.headline: Every occupied position gets its own mould base.
views.note: Each base carries its own ejection, its own cooling circuit and its own maintenance history. The commodity sizes are correctly served. The tail is paid for at the same price and never earns it back.

views.name: Dedicated head, modular tail
views.headline: High cavitation where the volume is. Shared frames where it is not.
views.note: A standardised frame stays in the machine while cavity and core inserts change. You buy cores and cavities rather than complete mould bases, and the toolroom's machining hours go into the inserts.

notes.heading: The head
notes.body: Elbows, tees and sockets at 20, 25 and 32 mm run effectively without stopping. Small projected area, short flow paths, continuous demand. This is the only geometry in the range where cavity count directly divides the machine hour, and it absorbs high cavitation without argument. Metal Form has built tooling to 46 cavities.

notes.heading: The tail
notes.body: A reducing tee at 90 mm may run three times a year. A wall-plate elbow runs in campaigns. These parts cannot carry a dedicated mould base, and building one for them is the most common way a tooling budget disappears without producing anything.

notes.heading: The agreement
notes.body: Whichever route a part takes, every socket in the matrix has to agree with the same pipe. A frame does not relax that requirement. It only changes where the machining hours go.

range.close: Balance the layout before adding cavities. A 32-cavity tool that fills unevenly is a 24-cavity tool with eight rejects, and it will be paid for as if it were 32.

mechanism.heading: The undercut decides the mechanism. The mechanism decides the cycle.
mechanism.body: Nearly every fitting has something that will not simply eject: an internal groove, a moulded thread, a sealing gland, a 360° feature. At that point the tool stops being a container and becomes a mechanism. The cost, the cycle, the downtime and a large share of the field failures all originate there. This is the section a fittings engineer reads first, so it is written flat.

options.name: Collapsible core
options.summary: A slotted steel tube whose segments retract radially, releasing a 360° internal feature without rotating anything.
options.figureLabel: Collapsible core · plan section and side section

legend.text: Slotted segments. The standard design uses twelve; dovetail designs use six larger segments that can be repaired individually.
Centre pin. It withdraws first; the segments then collapse inward onto it.
Collapse travel. This is what releases the groove, the gland or the partial thread.
Head space between the core flange and the centre-pin flange. Held exactly, or the mechanism does not collapse correctly.

options.name: Unscrewing core
options.summary: A rotating core, usually rack-and-pinion driven, that threads itself out of the moulded thread it formed.

legend.text: Pinion on the core shaft.
Rack. Its stroke sets the rotation, and every cavity in the layout has to stay synchronised with it.
Thread form on the core. Full form, which is the reason this mechanism exists.
Moulded part. It has to be held against rotation while the core turns out of it.

compare.label: The two mechanisms on the same rows

rows.a: 360° grooves, glands and partial threads. Published mini-core data reaches down to around Ø 10.8 mm and up to 80% full thread.
rows.b: Full thread form, including forms a collapsing segment cannot shut off.

rows.a: Published comparisons put collapsible cores as much as 30% faster than unscrewing mechanisms.
rows.b: Slower. The core has to rotate clear before the part can be ejected.

rows.a: Segments, centre pin, flanges. Twelve segments as standard, six on dovetail designs.
rows.b: Rack, pinion, bearings, seals, gearbox, and the synchronisation between cavities.

rows.a: Each core is matched to a numbered centre pin. Cores are not interchangeable between positions in the tool.
rows.b: Rotation count and timing across every cavity in the layout.

rows.a: Loss of head space, damaged segments, a segment rebuilt onto the wrong pin, flash at the lines where twelve pieces of steel meet.
rows.b: Broken rollers, damaged racks, water and oil leaks. On the part: scuffing, ovality, flash and grease contamination.

rows.a: Segment repair is the routine job. Dovetail designs are repaired one segment at a time.
rows.b: Described in published sources as among the most complex moulds built, and the most maintenance-intensive mechanism in a moulding hall.

compare.source: Comparative figures in this ledger are published industry practice, not Metal Form measurements.

third.heading: Side ports, stripping and where each stops
third.body: Branch ports on tees, crosses and manifolds are slides. They set the parting line before anything else in the tool does, which is why they are decided first and not last. A shallow snap or a low bead can be stripped over — bumped off — using the material's own elasticity, and that is the cheapest answer when the feature is genuinely shallow and the resin genuinely forgiving. Pushed beyond that, it stops being ejection and becomes a crack propagator.

mechanism.close: We specify the mechanism against your geometry and against the maintenance your own hall can carry. Where we would not use a mechanism on your part, we say so at the quotation rather than after it.

thread.heading: A tapered thread seals on its flanks. A parallel thread needs a gland.
thread.body: Two threads that look alike on a drawing behave nothing alike in a fitting, and they demand different steel. The taper seals by interference as it engages. The parallel thread does not seal at all on its own — something else has to, and that something is a groove, a face or an elastomer. Getting this wrong produces a fitting that assembles, passes a glance and weeps in a wall.

figures.name: Tapered thread
figures.note: The bore converges. Engagement tightens on the flanks, and the seal is made by the thread itself.

legend.text: Taper on the pitch line.
Flank interference. This is the sealing surface.
Shut-off in the tool lands on the flanks, which is what makes this form demanding to cut and demanding to maintain.

figures.name: Parallel thread
figures.note: The bore stays parallel. The thread carries load and nothing else. A washer, a face or an O-ring does the sealing.

legend.text: Parallel crest line.
Face or washer seat. The seal is here, not on the thread.
The boss that carries hoop stress when an installer over-torques it. Cracking here is a design outcome, not an installer error.

figures.name: O-ring gland
figures.figureLabel: O-ring gland in a bore · section
figures.note: A 360° groove in a bore. Nothing strips over it cleanly at working depth, so the gland is what puts a collapsible core into the tool.

legend.text: Groove width.
Groove depth. It sets compression: under-compressed weeps, over-compressed takes a set.
Corner condition. Sharp corners cut the seal; soft corners let it extrude.
The elastomer, compressed between gland and mating bore.

thread.ledgerLabel: The feature, and the steel that forms it
ledgerColumns: What has to be in the tool

ledger.v: Unscrewing core with the taper cut into it. Shut-off lands on the thread flanks.
Unscrewing core, or a collapsible core where the form allows the segments to shut off cleanly.
Split cavity on the parting line, or an unscrewing sleeve where the split line cannot be tolerated.
Collapsible core. The groove is a 360° undercut and it does not strip.
Collapsible core for the gland, slides for the release-collar features, and a bore finish that the grab ring can live with.
Insert-carrying tool. Insert location, anti-rotation against the knurl, and shut-off on the insert's own flanks.

ledger.k: Branch port on a tee or manifold
ledger.v: Slide or side core. It fixes the parting line for the whole tool.

insert.heading: Where the polymer meets the metal
insert.body: A threaded adapter is the interface between a plastic system and a metal one, and it fails in two documented ways. The insert pulls or spins out because the polymer never gripped the knurl. Or the boss around it splits, because an installer applied more torque than the hoop stress in that wall could carry. Both are decided at design: knurl engagement, insert location, wall around the insert, and whether the tool shuts off on the insert cleanly enough to keep flash off the thread. Insert loading also changes the economics of the cell, because a person or a robot now has to place metal in the tool on every shot.

material.heading: The resin chooses the runner, the steel and the vent.
material.body: There is no house recipe that survives contact with four different polymers. PVC punishes residence time. Polypropylene punishes uneven cooling. PE100 punishes residual stress. Each of them changes the runner decision, the steel decision and the venting decision, and getting the order wrong is expensive in a different way each time.

rows.name: PVC · PVC-U
rows.window: Melt in the region of 173–190 °C. Above roughly 200 °C it degrades and releases HCl.
rows.runner: Cold runner as the conservative default. Long residence in a heated manifold is a real degradation risk.
rows.steel: Corrosion resistance before hardness. Stainless or plated cavity surfaces.
rows.risk: Black specks, burns, and cavity corrosion from the degradation products themselves.

rows.name: PP · PP-R
rows.window: Semi-crystalline. Mould temperature is a live trade between surface, warpage and cycle, and it should be decided per part rather than discovered in production.
rows.shrink: Typically 1–2.5%, moving with cooling rate and wall thickness.
rows.runner: Hot runner pays back at commodity volumes. Valve gating gives pack and gate-freeze control on a thick socket land.
rows.steel: Polish and draft on deep parallel sockets. Ejection is a finish problem before it is a force problem.
rows.vent: Positioned at the last areas to fill — the heel of an elbow, the branch of a tee.
rows.risk: Ovality from uneven cooling of the socket land. No process setting makes it round again.

rows.name: PE100
rows.window: Buried systems and electrofusion. Stress-crack resistance is the governing property, not stiffness.
rows.shrink: High and cooling-dependent, as with PP.
rows.runner: Hot runner at volume. Gate position chosen against residual stress rather than against convenience.
rows.steel: Bore concentricity on coupler bodies; coil seat geometry on electrofusion parts.
rows.vent: Standard polyolefin practice, sized to the last fill area.
rows.risk: Residual moulded-in stress meeting sustained load and an aggressive medium. Environmental stress cracking.

rows.name: PEX system polymers
rows.window: Polysulfone-family polymers, and brass on the metal variants. High melt temperature, tight drying.
rows.runner: Hot runner with careful residence control.
rows.steel: High-temperature-capable surfaces; insert location where the body is brass-cored.
rows.vent: Sized for a high-viscosity, high-temperature melt.
rows.risk: In the field rather than in the tool: acetone-bearing solvent cleaners, UV and spray foam are documented attackers of these polymers.

rows.name: ABS
rows.window: Above-ground and underground drainage. Wide and forgiving.
rows.runner: Either route. Volume and colour-change frequency decide it.
rows.steel: Standard tool steels. Polish where a solvent-weld socket needs a clean bore.
rows.risk: Weld lines at branch intersections on large drainage bodies, where two fronts meet in a part nobody pressure-tests until it is buried.

material.note: One rule holds across all five. Datasheet shrinkage is a starting hypothesis, not a dimension. The first cavity is cut steel-safe and corrected against real parts, because a fitting family has to agree with itself and a handbook number will not deliver that.
material.source: Processing figures in this ledger are published industry practice, not Metal Form measurements.

agreement.heading: A socket that is not round is a joint that is not made.
agreement.body: Socket fusion melts the pipe outside and the socket bore together and pushes them home. Uneven contact prevents seating. The joint looks made, passes visual inspection and leaks later. Ovality and socket-depth inconsistency are the two dimensional failures in this sector that reach the customer's site rather than your scrap bin — which makes them commercial damage rather than yield loss.

figA.label: Socket bore, every cavity overlaid
figA.note: One tool, many cavities, one nominal bore. The spread is what a mould can hold or fail to hold. The out-of-round profile is the one that will not seat.

legend.text: Nominal bore.
Cavity-to-cavity spread. Invisible in one sample, decisive across a shipment.
Out of round. This one is dimensionally inside its diameter band and still will not make a joint.

figB.label: Socket and pipe end · engagement section
figB.note: The functional dimensions are the ones nobody photographs: depth of engagement, the interference along it, and whether the bore is round for the whole of it.

legend.text: Depth of engagement.
Interference along the engagement — deliberate, and the reason a solvent-weld socket makes a cemented joint rather than a glued gap.
The fusion or cement zone. It only exists where the two surfaces actually touch.

tolerance.v: dn / en — nominal outside diameter divided by wall thickness. The sector's shorthand for wall class.
PP-R Ø20–63 by hand, up to Ø125 with jigs. Heater setpoint published at 260 ± 10 °C.

agreement.source: These figures are quoted from published material on PP-R piping and its standards — DIN 8077, DIN 8078, EN ISO 15874 and DVS 2207. They are cited here as the standards' figures. They are not a Metal Form capability statement and not a tolerance we are offering.
can: Wall uniformity and core position under fill pressure
Cooling symmetry around the socket land, which is where ovality is won or lost
Gate position, and therefore where the weld line lands
Vent position, so the last area to fill is not the burnt one
cannot: The pressure class the finished fitting is declared to
Whether the resin you selected performs over decades at temperature
Whether the installer scraped the pipe before an electrofusion joint
Whether the site heater was actually at its setpoint
Whether the SDR of the pipe and the fitting were specified to match
agreement.close: Attack ovality at the cooling layout, not at the process. An unevenly cooled socket shrinks unevenly, and no amount of tuning makes it round again.

economics.heading: Three numbers are paid on every shot.
economics.body: Grams per part. Seconds per shot. Parts per shot. The mould price is paid once. These three are paid for the entire life of the range, and they are what your cost per thousand is actually made of. A buyer who compares two tooling quotations without comparing those three has compared the wrong thing.

numbers.name: Grams per part
numbers.note: Resin is the largest recurring line in the operation and it never stops running. On most catalogue fittings the wall thickness was inherited from a drawing nobody has re-examined since it was first made.

numbers.name: Seconds per shot
numbers.note: In a thick-walled fitting, cooling is most of the cycle. Published guidance puts PP sections above 3 mm at twenty to thirty seconds of cooling alone. Cooling laid out around the socket land, not around the tool, is where that time is recovered.

numbers.name: Parts per shot
numbers.note: Cavitation is the divisor on machine hour, labour and overhead. It only helps if the layout fills and cools evenly, which is why balance is engineered before cavity count is chosen.

outputs.k: Resin in parts, tonnes per year

economics.deltasHeading: And one step on each input is worth
economics.disclaimer: The figures above are arbitrary and chosen to be legible. They are the shape of the arithmetic, not a quotation, not a benchmark, and not a result being claimed on your part. Your numbers are your own and they are the only ones that matter.
economics.lostHeading: Where the money actually goes missing

lost.v: A legacy drawing sets a wall, the wall sets the grams, and the grams are bought again on every shot for eight years. Nobody re-opens the file because the part works.

lost.k: Cycle padded to hide a sink
lost.v: Two or three seconds added at the machine to suppress a sink mark that a cooling revision would have removed permanently. The process technician is not wrong. The tool is.

lost.k: Five bases doing one frame's work
lost.v: Five standalone moulds built for five variants of the same body, where one standardised frame and five insert sets would have covered the same catalogue positions.

economics.close: Send the part and the dimension table. We will tell you what those three numbers currently are on your geometry, and which of them moves without touching a dimension your catalogue depends on.

boundary.heading: A mould does not confer a pressure rating.
boundary.body: This is the clearest line on the page and it is worth stating before anyone asks for it. We build tooling and we can produce components. What the finished fitting is approved to carry is not ours to declare, and a supplier who implies otherwise has told you something useful about themselves.

boundary.statement: We build the tool and we can produce the part. Approval of the finished fitting for a pressure class or a potable-water application belongs to you, your material and your certification body. We hold no product certification, we do not test fittings, and we will not claim a standard on your behalf. Every published figure quoted on this page belongs to the source or the standard it came from, and is cited as context rather than as capability.

start.heading: One tool, one top-selling size, no duplicate.
start.body: Ask which single mould, if it stopped tomorrow, would stop the plant. In a fitting range there is almost always one — a 25 mm elbow or a 32 mm tee carrying a disproportionate share of revenue on one tool, with no backup and often no CAD. Manufacturers in this sector already run dual sources on resin and on purchased components so they can shift demand when a route closes. Tooling rarely gets the same treatment.
start.auditHeading: Six questions worth answering before you need the answers

audit.q: Is there a duplicate tool for your highest-volume part number?
audit.c: If there is not, one mechanism failure is a stopped catalogue number and a standing distributor order you cannot fill.

audit.q: Do you hold the 3D data, or only the steel?
audit.c: Steel without CAD cannot be rebuilt, revised or duplicated anywhere, by anyone, including you.

audit.q: Is the original mould maker still trading, and do they still answer?
audit.c: A range built in 2011 by a shop that has since closed has no spares route and no revision route.

audit.q: Do the parts coming off the tool still match the drawing?
audit.c: Tools drift. The pipe your customers weld to agrees with the part, not with the drawing in the file.

audit.q: Where are the spare cores and segments, and how long to replace one?
audit.c: A collapsible core segment matched to a numbered pin is not a stock item anywhere in the world.

audit.q: What is your tooling lead time against your construction season?
audit.c: A tool ordered in February that lands in October was bought for a season that has already closed.

From production parts you send us where the data does not exist, so the duplicate agrees with the pipe your customers already weld to.
By reverse engineering a sample where only steel and parts survive.
Where the original tool has drifted, the duplicate is the opportunity to correct it rather than to replicate the drift.
This is readiness, not reserved capacity. Capacity is reserved by contract or it is not reserved, and we will say which.

Material and grade, because the resin decides runner, steel, surface and venting

Which part numbers are variants of the same body, so a modular frame can be assessed against separate tools
Target machine, tonnage and platen size if the tool has to run on equipment you already own
Brass insert drawings where inserts are involved
Parts from the existing tool, if this is a replacement or a second source

Which part numbers we would give a dedicated tool, and which we would put on a shared frame
A part-weight and cycle assessment on the geometry you sent

Which mechanism we would not use on your part, and why

items.title: Core mechanism selection
bullets: Collapsible core — for 360° internal grooves, glands and partial threads. Standard designs use twelve slotted segments; dovetail designs use six larger segments that are individually repairable.
Published mini collapsible cores reach down to around 10.8 mm diameter and cover up to 80% full thread.
Head space between core flange and centre-pin flange has to be held precisely, and each core is matched to a numbered pin. They cannot be swapped between positions in the tool.
Unscrewing core — for full thread form where a collapsible core cannot shut off. Published sources describe unscrewing moulds as among the most complex injection moulds built.
Documented unscrewing failure modes: broken rollers, damaged racks, water and oil leaks; on the part, scuffing, ovality, flash and grease contamination.
Slides and side cores — for branch ports on tees, crosses and manifolds. They set the parting line before anything else does.
Stripping and bumping-off — viable only on shallow features and forgiving resins. Beyond that it is a crack propagator.
We specify against your geometry and your maintenance capability, and we will name the mechanism we would not use.
items.source: Mechanism figures and failure modes in this panel are published industry practice, not Metal Form measurements.

items.title: Runner, cooling and venting in a fitting tool
bullets: PVC processes in a narrow window around 173–190 °C and degrades above roughly 200 °C, releasing HCl. That is a tool-corrosion problem as well as an operator-safety one.
It argues for cold runners on PVC, short residence, corrosion-resistant or plated cavity surfaces, and venting in the region of 0.03–0.05 mm.

Polyolefins at commodity volumes usually justify hot runners: an optimised cold runner still carries 50–100% more cycle time, because the runner has to cool alongside the part, and it produces regrind on every shot.
Valve gating gives pack and gate-freeze control on a thick socket land that a hot tip cannot.
The SKU tail argues the other way. Low volume and frequent colour change favour cold runners, so a range of any size ends up with both.
Cooling is most of the cycle in a fitting. Published guidance puts thick PP sections above 3 mm at twenty to thirty seconds of cooling on their own.
Cooling layout belongs around the socket land, not around the tool. That is where cycle time is actually won, and it is what standard fitting moulds most often under-invest in.
Design guidance published for PVC: wall transitions within 10–15% of nominal, draft 0.5–1° on vertical walls, corner radii at 25–75% of wall.
items.source: Processing figures in this panel are published industry practice, not Metal Form measurements.
